--- title: "Notebook 1 — Building a silicon sample" subtitle: "LLMSS 2026, Workshop 1 (AIPOP) · Hong Kong, 13 October 2026" output: html_document: toc: true toc_float: true df_print: kable --- ## What you will do A digital twin is not a random person. It is **a slot in a measured population frame**, filled by a record and then given attitudes by a matched survey respondent. This notebook builds the frame and fills 400 of those slots for Ohio, then audits what you drew. By the end you will have: 1. read a **stage-1 frame** — who lives in each Ohio district, from the ACS; 2. read a **stage-2 frame** — how each of those cells voted in November 2024; 3. checked the frame against the **certified** 2024 result; 4. collapsed it to a **teaching mini-frame**; 5. drawn **400 synthetic skeletons** by probability-proportional-to-size sampling; 6. **audited** the drawn margins, and raked them to the acceptance standard. Nothing here calls a language model. That is the point: *the composition of a panel is fixed by census and certified-result data before any model is involved.* The model never chooses who is in the panel. > **A note on what you are drawing.** There are two routes to a skeleton. The > stronger one starts from a state **voter file**: the official list of > registered voters, with each person's county, registration and turnout > history. Ohio publishes one, and the Talking to Machines panel draws **real > registrants** from it into these cells. Working with a voter file requires a > licence and ethical care, because every row is a real, identifiable person. > This notebook takes the other route: it draws **synthetic skeletons** > directly from the census frame. Section 7 shows what the registrant route adds. **How to read this notebook.** Every table and figure the code prints has a number (Table 1.1, Figure 1.1, …), given in bold just above the code that prints it. When the text quotes a number, it says which table it comes from, and which row or column to look at. The first block loads the three R packages the notebook uses and fixes the random seed, so everyone draws the same panel. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(arrow) library(data.table) library(ggplot2) DATA <- file.path("..", "data") set.seed(20261013L) # every draw in this notebook is seeded and reproducible ``` ::: --- ## 1. Stage 1 — who lives here Stage 1 is the American Community Survey (ACS) 2019–2023 five-year PUMS: the individual responses behind the ACS, for adults 18+, allocated from their PUMA (the smallest area the ACS publishes) to congressional districts. The block below loads it as a table called `sf1`, prints its size (rows, columns), and prints its first three rows. **Table 1.1.** `sf1`, the stage-1 frame: size, then the first three rows. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf1 <- as.data.table(read_parquet(file.path(DATA, "SF_OH.parquet"))) dim(sf1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 23798 12 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(sf1, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|state |CD119 |gender |ethnicity |age_bins |marital_status |college_grad |hh_income |internet | citizen| N| n_pums| |:-----|:-----|:------|:---------|:--------|:--------------|:------------------------------|:------------|:--------------------------|-------:|----:|------:| |OH |07 |F |White |65+ |Not Married |Does not have a College Degree |[min, 25000) |Has access to the internet | 1| 9950| 640| |OH |04 |F |White |25-34 |Not Married |Does not have a College Degree |[min, 25000) |Has access to the internet | 1| 2973| 141| |OH |11 |M |White |35-44 |Not Married |Has a College Degree |[min, 25000) |Has access to the internet | 1| 390| 30|
::: ::: Each row of Table 1.1 is a **cell**: one combination of district (`CD119`), sex, ethnicity, age band, marital status, degree, household income, internet access and citizenship. The line above the table gives the size: 23,798 cells and 12 columns. The last two columns are the ones that matter: - `n_pums` is how many ACS respondents fall in the cell (640 in the first row); - `N` is how many Ohio adults those respondents stand for (9,950 in the first row). Each respondent carries a **person weight**, the number of people they represent, and `N` is the sum of those weights. The ACS is a sample, but the Census Bureau calibrates its person weights to independent population controls. So adding up `N` reproduces the **ACS's own published estimates** for Ohio directly, without raking afterwards. They are estimates, with sampling error, not a census count. The next block adds up `N` over all cells, and over citizens only (`citizen == 1`). **Table 1.2.** `sf1` summed: number of cells, adults, and citizen adults. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf1[, .(cells = .N, adults = format(sum(N), big.mark = ","), citizen_adults = format(sum(N[citizen == 1]), big.mark = ","))] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| cells|adults |citizen_adults | |-----:|:---------|:--------------| | 23798|9,170,227 |8,931,251 |
::: ::: Table 1.2 shows 9,170,227 adults, of whom 8,931,251 are citizens (column `citizen_adults`). Everything from stage 2 on uses the **citizen adults**, the people who can vote. The same 8,931,251 is the size of the frame Notebook 3 post-stratifies to. **Exercise 1.1.** The frame carries every Ohio district. How many citizen adults does the frame put in OH-09, and what share of them hold a college degree? Write a block that keeps the citizen cells of district 09 in `sf1` and sums their `N`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # your code here ``` ::: --- ## 2. Stage 2 — how those cells voted Stage 1 says who lives in a district. Stage 2 says **how each cell voted in November 2024**, in four classes: Democratic, Republican, other, and stayed home. It is a multinomial logit fitted in Stan over the CES 2024 vote-validated release, with the certified district result as an area predictor and hierarchical effects for sex, ethnicity, college, age, income, state and district. Model probabilities are then computed for every stage-1 cell and **raked** within each district so that D, R, other and stay-home totals equal the certified result. You do not fit this model here. It was fitted once, and this notebook reads its result: `SF_extended_OH.parquet`, the stage-1 cells with the four vote classes attached. The block below loads it as `sf2` and prints its size and first three rows. **Table 1.3.** `sf2`, the stage-2 frame: size, then the first three rows. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf2 <- as.data.table(read_parquet(file.path(DATA, "SF_extended_OH.parquet"))) dim(sf2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 9467 18 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(sf2, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|state |area |TX26 |gender |ethnicity |college_grad |age_bins |hh_income | N|area_key | p_D| p_R| p_Other| p_stay home| N_D| N_R| N_Other| N_stay| |:-----|:-----|:----|:------|:---------|:------------------------------|:--------|:------------|----:|:--------|---------:|---------:|---------:|-----------:|---------:|--------:|---------:|--------:| |OH |OH-01 |NA |M |White |Does not have a College Degree |18-24 |[min, 25000) | 4832|OH-01 | 0.1224127| 0.6444133| 0.0321832| 0.2009908| 77.64800| 457.8466| 19.116852| 4277.389| |OH |OH-01 |NA |F |White |Does not have a College Degree |18-24 |[min, 25000) | 5336|OH-01 | 0.1166994| 0.5565905| 0.0337429| 0.2929672| 58.74093| 313.8050| 15.905172| 4947.549| |OH |OH-01 |NA |F |White |Does not have a College Degree |45-54 |[min, 25000) | 1242|OH-01 | 0.3879578| 0.5552714| 0.0088293| 0.0479415| 183.44484| 294.0886| 3.909577| 760.557|
::: ::: `sf2` has 9,467 rows (the line above Table 1.3). It keeps **citizens only**, and drops marital status and internet access from the key, so it has fewer cells than `sf1`. The district is now in the column `area` (`OH-01`, …). `N` is still the number of citizen adults in the cell, and each row gains two sets of columns: - `p_D`, `p_R`, `p_Other`, `p_stay home`: the model's probability that a person in this cell voted Democratic, Republican, other, or stayed home; - `N_D`, `N_R`, `N_Other`, `N_stay`: how many of the cell's `N` people fall in each class, after raking to the certified result. In the first row of Table 1.3, 4,832 men aged 18–24 in OH-01 split into about 78 Democratic voters, 458 Republican, 19 other and 4,277 who stayed home. The four counts split `N` between them, so they must add back up to it. The next block prints the largest gap between `N_D + N_R + N_Other + N_stay` and `N` across all 9,467 rows: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the four counts should sum back to the cell size sf2[, max(abs(N_D + N_R + N_Other + N_stay - N))] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 7.275958e-11 ``` ::: ::: The answer is of the order of 0.0000000001: rounding, so the counts add up. **Exercise 2.1.** Ohio's turnout and two-party split, straight off the frame. Write a block that sums the columns of `sf2` over the whole state: citizen adults, 2024 voters (`N_D + N_R + N_Other`), turnout, and Harris's share of the two-party vote. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # your code here ``` ::: --- ## 3. Does the frame know the answer? Check it against certified results This is the first validation the project runs on every frame. After raking, district totals are exact *by construction* — so the honest check is whether the numbers you have match the certified results you were raked to, and whether the **shape** of the vote across districts is right. The first block loads the certified 2024 presidential result by district as `cert`, and prints Harris's two-party share for Ohio's 15 districts. **Table 1.4.** `cert`: the certified 2024 result. `certified_harris_2p` is Harris's share of the two-party (Harris + Trump) vote; `cvap` is the district's citizen voting-age population. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cert <- fread(file.path(DATA, "predictor_cd119_2024.csv"), colClasses = list(character = "CD119"))[state == "OH"] cert[, .(CD119, certified_harris_2p = 1 - pct_trump, cvap)][order(CD119)] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|CD119 | certified_harris_2p| cvap| |:-----|-------------------:|------:| |01 | 0.5319971| 582434| |02 | 0.2602888| 608007| |03 | 0.7032872| 563590| |04 | 0.3145881| 597139| |05 | 0.3523275| 605047| |06 | 0.3303679| 611341| |07 | 0.4463461| 607056| |08 | 0.3804773| 579017| |09 | 0.4661307| 598611| |10 | 0.4710201| 595475| |11 | 0.7773096| 589067| |12 | 0.3349139| 602482| |13 | 0.5002336| 605625| |14 | 0.4095340| 619946| |15 | 0.4535597| 566414|
::: ::: The next block computes the same share from the frame: for each district, the Democratic voters in `sf2` over its Democratic plus Republican voters. It puts the two side by side in a table called `cmp`, with the difference in percentage points. **Table 1.5.** `cmp`: frame against certified, by district. `diff_pp` is the frame minus the certified share, in points. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} byCD <- sf2[, .(frame_harris_2p = sum(N_D) / sum(N_D + N_R)), by = .(CD119 = sub("OH-", "", area))] cmp <- merge(byCD, cert[, .(CD119, certified_harris_2p = 1 - pct_trump)], by = "CD119") cmp[, diff_pp := 100 * (frame_harris_2p - certified_harris_2p)] cmp[order(CD119)] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|CD119 | frame_harris_2p| certified_harris_2p| diff_pp| |:-----|---------------:|-------------------:|--------:| |01 | 0.5319972| 0.5319971| 9.50e-06| |02 | 0.2602889| 0.2602888| 7.30e-06| |03 | 0.7032873| 0.7032872| 7.00e-06| |04 | 0.3145882| 0.3145881| 1.16e-05| |05 | 0.3523276| 0.3523275| 5.80e-06| |06 | 0.3303679| 0.3303679| 2.60e-06| |07 | 0.4463462| 0.4463461| 8.20e-06| |08 | 0.3804774| 0.3804773| 8.90e-06| |09 | 0.4661308| 0.4661307| 9.10e-06| |10 | 0.4710202| 0.4710201| 6.50e-06| |11 | 0.7773097| 0.7773096| 5.20e-06| |12 | 0.3349140| 0.3349139| 5.30e-06| |13 | 0.5002337| 0.5002336| 1.34e-05| |14 | 0.4095341| 0.4095340| 9.00e-06| |15 | 0.4535598| 0.4535597| 9.50e-06|
::: ::: Every value in the `diff_pp` column of Table 1.5 is about 0.00001 points: the frame reproduces the certified result exactly. The last block plots the same two columns against each other, saves the plot to `figures/`, and shows it. **Figure 1.1.** Frame against certified Harris share, one point per district. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_frame <- ggplot(cmp, aes(100 * certified_harris_2p, 100 * frame_harris_2p)) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") + geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "#2c6e9e") + geom_text(aes(label = CD119), nudge_y = 1.1, size = 3, colour = "grey30") + labs(x = "Certified Harris share, two-party (%)", y = "Frame Harris share, two-party (%)", title = "Ohio stage-2 frame against the certified 2024 result", subtitle = "Exact by construction after raking — this checks the rake, not the model") + coord_equal() + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ggsave(file.path("..", "figures", "oh_frame_vs_certified.png"), p_frame, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 200) p_frame ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01_frame_and_sample_files/figure-html/frame-vs-certified-plot-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: > **Discussion.** Why is Figure 1.1 *not* evidence that the method works? What > would be? (The answer: a held-out election — > New Jersey, November 2025 — that appears nowhere in the pipeline. We come back > to it in Notebook 3.) --- ## 4. The mini-frame The project's registrant draw uses `district × county × sex × ethnicity × age` as its cell key, with the vote class assigned inside each cell. **County is not in the ACS frame** — it enters only from the voter file, which splits each frame cell across counties by its own composition. Since you are drawing synthetically, your key is: ``` district × sex × ethnicity × age × college × vote2024 ``` The mini-frame is **not a subset**. It holds the same citizen adults as `sf2`, under a different key: the vote class moves from four count columns (`N_D`, `N_R`, `N_Other`, `N_stay`) into the key, and household income drops out. Same people, re-keyed. Why can a synthetic draw not have county? The ACS does not publish it. The smallest geography in the PUMS is the PUMA, and PUMAs and counties do not nest: a rural PUMA combines several whole counties, and an urban county is split across several PUMAs. Placing a synthetic person in a county would mean inventing that joint distribution. A voter file records each registrant's county directly. This is worth pausing on. Leaving county out is a real defect. When the project's panels were drawn without it, a county's realised partisan composition was an uncontrolled by-product of the draw, and Passaic County, New Jersey came out **13.4 points too Democratic**. Adding county to the cell key brought the state's county error from 2.98 to 1.73 points. Your synthetic sample cannot have this control, and it is the clearest illustration of what a voter file buys you. The block below builds the mini-frame as a table called `mini`. It turns each `sf2` row into four rows, one per vote class, each with that class's count as its `N`; drops the empty ones; adds up rows that now share the same key (which is where income disappears); and sorts them. It prints the number of cells and people, then the first five rows. **Table 1.6.** `mini`, the mini-frame: size, then the first five cells. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mini <- melt( sf2, id.vars = c("area", "gender", "ethnicity", "age_bins", "college_grad"), measure.vars = c("N_D", "N_R", "N_Other", "N_stay"), variable.name = "vote2024", value.name = "N" ) mini[, vote2024 := factor(vote2024, levels = c("N_D", "N_R", "N_Other", "N_stay"), labels = c("D", "R", "Other", "stay"))] mini <- mini[N > 0, .(N = sum(N)), by = .(cd = area, gender, ethnicity, age_bins, college_grad, vote2024)] setorder(mini, cd, vote2024, ethnicity, age_bins, gender) cat(sprintf("%s cells, %s citizen adults\n", format(nrow(mini), big.mark = ","), format(round(sum(mini$N)), big.mark = ","))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 9,540 cells, 8,931,251 citizen adults ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(mini, 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|cd |gender |ethnicity |age_bins |college_grad |vote2024 | N| |:-----|:------|:---------|:--------|:------------------------------|:--------|---------:| |OH-01 |F |Asian |18-24 |Does not have a College Degree |D | 13.83218| |OH-01 |F |Asian |18-24 |Has a College Degree |D | 19.69479| |OH-01 |M |Asian |18-24 |Does not have a College Degree |D | 26.58007| |OH-01 |M |Asian |18-24 |Has a College Degree |D | 18.21969| |OH-01 |F |Asian |25-34 |Has a College Degree |D | 569.90428|
::: ::: The line above Table 1.6 confirms it: 9,540 cells holding the same 8,931,251 citizen adults as `sf2`. Each row is a cell of the key above, and `N` is the number of people in it: the first row is 14 Asian women aged 18–24 without a degree in OH-01 who voted Democratic. --- ## 5. Draw 400 skeletons **Systematic probability-proportional-to-size.** Sort the cells, take the cumulative population, lay down 400 equally spaced points along it, and take the cell each point lands in. Compared with drawing 400 independent cells this gives margins on the leading sort keys that are exact to ±1 — which is why the project's draw uses it. The block below writes that procedure as a function, `draw_pps()`, and runs it on `mini` to draw 400 skeletons into a table called `panel`. Inside the function: `step` is the population between two picks; `start` is a random point inside the first step; `picks` are the 400 equally spaced points; `cum` is the running total of `N` down the sorted cells; and `findInterval()` finds the cell each point lands in. Each pick gets an id, `oh_syn_0001` to `oh_syn_0400`. The block prints the size of `panel` and its first five rows. **Table 1.7.** `panel`, your 400 skeletons: size, then the first five. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} draw_pps <- function(frame, n, seed = 20261013L) { set.seed(seed) f <- copy(frame)[N > 0] step <- sum(f$N) / n start <- runif(1, 0, step) picks <- start + step * (0:(n - 1)) f[, cum := cumsum(N)] idx <- findInterval(picks, c(0, f$cum), rightmost.closed = TRUE) out <- f[idx] out[, `:=`(cum = NULL, N = NULL)] out[, twin_id := sprintf("oh_syn_%04d", seq_len(.N))] setcolorder(out, "twin_id") out[] } panel <- draw_pps(mini, n = 400) dim(panel) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 400 7 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(panel, 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|twin_id |cd |gender |ethnicity |age_bins |college_grad |vote2024 | |:-----------|:-----|:------|:---------|:--------|:------------------------------|:--------| |oh_syn_0001 |OH-01 |F |Asian |35-44 |Has a College Degree |D | |oh_syn_0002 |OH-01 |M |Black |45-54 |Does not have a College Degree |D | |oh_syn_0003 |OH-01 |F |Black |65+ |Has a College Degree |D | |oh_syn_0004 |OH-01 |F |White |25-34 |Does not have a College Degree |D | |oh_syn_0005 |OH-01 |M |White |25-34 |Has a College Degree |D |
::: ::: Each row of Table 1.7 is one skeleton: the attributes of the cell its pick landed in, and nothing else. To picture the draw, the next block prints its arithmetic: the population between two picks, the median and largest cell, how many cells are bigger than one step (and so certain to be picked), and how many distinct cells the 400 picks landed in. **Table 1.8.** The draw in numbers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data.table(people = round(sum(mini$N)), people_per_pick = round(sum(mini$N) / 400), median_cell = round(median(mini$N)), largest_cell = round(max(mini$N)), cells_above_step = sum(mini$N >= sum(mini$N) / 400), distinct_cells = uniqueN(panel, by = c("cd", "gender", "ethnicity", "age_bins", "college_grad", "vote2024"))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| people| people_per_pick| median_cell| largest_cell| cells_above_step| distinct_cells| |-------:|---------------:|-----------:|------------:|----------------:|--------------:| | 8931251| 22328| 50| 40057| 32| 389|
::: ::: Read Table 1.8 from left to right. 8,931,251 people over 400 picks is one pick every 22,328 people (`people_per_pick`). The cells are sorted, their populations added up into a running total, the first point falls at random inside the first 22,328, and each later point is one step further on. The median cell holds 50 people and the largest about 40,000, so only the 32 cells bigger than one step (`cells_above_step`) are certain to be picked. The 400 picks land in 389 distinct cells (`distinct_cells`): a few cells were picked twice. > **A pick is a person, not a cell.** The cell supplies the attributes; the pick > is one individual drawn from it. Two picks in the same cell are two different > people who happen to share a profile. The rest of the workshop rests on this: > each of your 400 skeletons stands for one Ohioan. Each skeleton then gets an integer age drawn uniformly within its band: 18–24 from 18 to 24, and 65+ from 65 to 89. That puts the average 65+ skeleton at 77, older than Ohio's real 65+ population. No margin changes, since the band is what gets raked, but every persona that states an age inherits it. The civic record is rendered explicitly as **not observed** — a synthetic skeleton has no turnout history, and the persona must say so rather than invent one. The block below adds both columns to `panel` (`age_lo` and `age_hi` are the ends of each band) and prints the first five skeletons again. **Table 1.9.** `panel` with ages, first five skeletons. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} age_lo <- c("18-24" = 18, "25-34" = 25, "35-44" = 35, "45-54" = 45, "55-64" = 55, "65+" = 65) age_hi <- c("18-24" = 24, "25-34" = 34, "35-44" = 44, "45-54" = 54, "55-64" = 64, "65+" = 89) panel[, age := mapply(function(a) sample(age_lo[[a]]:age_hi[[a]], 1), age_bins)] panel[, civic_record := "not observed (synthetic skeleton drawn from the ACS frame)"] head(panel[, .(twin_id, cd, gender, ethnicity, age, college_grad, vote2024)], 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|twin_id |cd |gender |ethnicity | age|college_grad |vote2024 | |:-----------|:-----|:------|:---------|---:|:------------------------------|:--------| |oh_syn_0001 |OH-01 |F |Asian | 35|Has a College Degree |D | |oh_syn_0002 |OH-01 |M |Black | 45|Does not have a College Degree |D | |oh_syn_0003 |OH-01 |F |Black | 75|Has a College Degree |D | |oh_syn_0004 |OH-01 |F |White | 28|Does not have a College Degree |D | |oh_syn_0005 |OH-01 |M |White | 28|Has a College Degree |D |
::: ::: --- ## 6. Audit what you drew A panel is only useful if it is the electorate in miniature. The project's acceptance standard is: **every one-way margin within 0.3 percentage points unweighted, and 0.00 weighted, with no cell short.** A **one-way margin** is the share of the panel in each category of one variable: the share that is female, the share in each age band, and so on. The audit compares your panel with the mini-frame. The mini-frame is `sf2` re-keyed, so its one-way margins are the full frame's: this is your panel against the Ohio frame. The block below writes the comparison as a function, `margin_check()`. For one variable it computes the share of `panel` in each category (`panel_share`), the share of `mini`'s people in the same category (`frame_share`), and the difference in points (`diff_pp`). It then runs it for the five audited variables and prints only the largest gap for each. **Table 1.10.** The audit, largest gap per variable (in percentage points). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} margin_check <- function(panel, frame, var) { p <- panel[, .(panel_share = .N / nrow(panel)), by = var] f <- frame[, .(frame_share = sum(N) / sum(frame$N)), by = var] m <- merge(p, f, by = var, all = TRUE) m[is.na(panel_share), panel_share := 0][is.na(frame_share), frame_share := 0] m[, diff_pp := 100 * (panel_share - frame_share)] m[order(-abs(diff_pp))] } for (v in c("gender", "ethnicity", "age_bins", "vote2024", "cd")) { cat("\n---", v, "— max |diff| =", sprintf("%.2f pp\n", max(abs(margin_check(panel, mini, v)$diff_pp)))) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` --- gender — max |diff| = 1.40 pp --- ethnicity — max |diff| = 1.00 pp --- age_bins — max |diff| = 1.50 pp --- vote2024 — max |diff| = 0.57 pp --- cd — max |diff| = 0.23 pp ``` ::: ::: Table 1.10 shows that only the district margin (`cd`, 0.23 points) clears the 0.3-point bar; sex, ethnicity, age and vote class do not. The next block prints the full comparison for two of them, every category, largest gap first. **Tables 1.11 and 1.12.** Vote class, then ethnicity: panel against frame. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} margin_check(panel, mini, "vote2024") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|vote2024 | panel_share| frame_share| diff_pp| |:--------|-----------:|-----------:|----------:| |Other | 0.0000| 0.0057329| -0.5732909| |stay | 0.3575| 0.3545108| 0.2989161| |R | 0.3575| 0.3560667| 0.1433315| |D | 0.2850| 0.2836896| 0.1310432|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} margin_check(panel, mini, "ethnicity") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

Write a block that runs `margin_check()` on `panel_4000` for the five variables of Table 1.10 and compares the largest gaps with your 400. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # your code here ``` ::: ### Raking the residual away Systematic PPS leaves rounding residue on the margins that are not the leading sort key. **Raking** removes it: each skeleton gets a weight, and the weights are adjusted one variable at a time, round after round, until the weighted shares match the frame's. The block below defines three functions: `rake()` computes the weights; `wmargin()` is the weighted version of the margin check; `report()` prints the range of the weights and the largest weighted gap for each variable. It then rakes `panel` on the five variables, stores the result in a new column, `weight`, and prints the report. **Table 1.13.** The raked 400-skeleton panel: weight range, then the largest weighted gap per variable. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rake <- function(panel, frame, vars, iters = 50) { w <- rep(1, nrow(panel)) for (i in seq_len(iters)) { for (v in vars) { tgt <- frame[, .(t = sum(N) / sum(frame$N)), by = v] cur <- data.table(lvl = panel[[v]], w = w)[, .(c = sum(w)), by = lvl][, c := c / sum(c)] setnames(cur, "lvl", v) f <- merge(cur, tgt, by = v)[, ratio := t / c] w <- w * f$ratio[match(panel[[v]], f[[v]])] } } w / mean(w) } MARGINS <- c("gender", "ethnicity", "age_bins", "vote2024", "cd") wmargin <- function(panel, frame, var) { p <- panel[, .(panel_share = sum(weight) / sum(panel$weight)), by = var] f <- frame[, .(frame_share = sum(N) / sum(frame$N)), by = var] merge(p, f, by = var, all = TRUE)[is.na(panel_share), panel_share := 0 ][, max(abs(100 * (panel_share - frame_share)))] } report <- function(panel, frame, label) { cat(label, sprintf("— weights %.2f–%.2f\n", min(panel$weight), max(panel$weight))) for (v in MARGINS) cat(sprintf(" %-10s weighted max |diff| = %.4f pp\n", v, wmargin(panel, frame, v))) } panel[, weight := rake(panel, mini, MARGINS)] report(panel, mini, "n = 400") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n = 400 — weights 0.74–1.26 gender weighted max |diff| = 0.0000 pp ethnicity weighted max |diff| = 0.1114 pp age_bins weighted max |diff| = 0.0000 pp vote2024 weighted max |diff| = 0.5733 pp cd weighted max |diff| = 0.0000 pp ``` ::: ::: In Table 1.13, two margins do not reach zero: `ethnicity` and `vote2024`. That is not a bug in the raking — it is a property of the sample you drew. Other is about 0.6% of Ohio's electorate (the `frame_share` of 0.0057 in Table 1.11), and 0.6% of 400 rounds to two twins; this draw got none. No weight can give an empty cell the right share, so the vote2024 margin cannot close, and raking it pushes the residual onto ethnicity. This is a hard limit of a small panel, not something to tune away. At the project's Tier C size the cell is populated and every margin closes. So the propensity steering which registrant fills a D or an R slot is estimated from the CES validated *primary* field. The block below prints the map the panel uses. **Table 1.19.** The partisan map: one row per type of voter-file record, with the weight each type gets for a Democratic (`p_D`), Republican (`p_R`) or other (`p_Other`) slot. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cat(readLines(file.path(DATA, "oh_pmap.csv")), sep = "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` cell,p_D,p_R,p_Other D.dp,0.962,0.038,0.05 D.none,0.962,0.038,0.05 R.rp,0.101,0.899,0.05 R.none,0.101,0.899,0.05 U.np_,0.5,0.5,0.05 U.none,0.479,0.521,0.05 M.np_,0.5,0.5,0.05 M.none,0.5,0.5,0.05 ``` ::: ::: Read the row `D.dp` in Table 1.19 as: a registrant who took a Democratic primary ballot is given a 0.962 weight for the Democratic slots. A simpler rule would be two fixed constants, say `.9` and `.05`. Used as competing selection weights, those are odds of 18:1 and behave as near-certainty rather than as the modest priors they look like. Estimating the weights per state from the CES validated file avoids that. The coherence check is the block headed `partisan_class (primary ballots) by vote2024` near the end of Table 1.16. In its `D` row, 52% of D-slot twins have a Democratic primary record (`dem_primary`) against 7% Republican (`rep_primary`); in its `R` row, 62% of R-slot twins have a Republican record against 2% Democratic. Note also the `no_primary` column: more than a third of D-slot twins (37%) have **no** primary record at all — for them the partisan class rests on the district and county rakes alone. ### Your sample against the real one Everything above differs, and yet the *composition* should not. Both are drawn to the same frame, so the vote-class shares of a 4,000-twin synthetic draw and the project's 4,000-registrant panel should agree with each other, and with the frame itself, which is the target both were drawn to. The block below computes the share of each vote class in three places: the frame (`mini`, column `frame`), your 4,000-skeleton draw (`panel_4000`, column `yours`), and the project's panel (column `project`).
